abla_{y}f(x,y),y^{\prime}-yangle- rac{\mu}{2}\lVert y^{\prime}-yVert^{2},\qquad y,y^{\prime}\in Y.}$ (2.3) (iii) The value function is bounded below: $\inf_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y)>-\infty.$ (2.4)

Definition 2.1 ( $\varepsilon$ -optimization stationary point) . For $\lambda>L$ and $\varepsilon>0$ , a point $x\in X$ is an $\varepsilon$ -optimization stationary point relative to $\lambda$ if $\lVert\nabla\Phi_{\lambda}(x)\rVert\leq\varepsilon.$ (2.9) A random point $Z\in X$ almost surely is $\varepsilon$ -optimization stationary in expectation relative to $\lambda$ if $\mathbb{E}\lVert\nabla\Phi_{\lambda}(Z)\rVert\leq\varepsilon.$

Definition 2.2 ( $\varepsilon$ -game stationary point) . For $\varepsilon>0$ , a pair $(x,y)\in X\times Y$ is an $\varepsilon$ -game stationary point of ( 2.1 ) if $\mathcal{R}(x,y)\leq\varepsilon.$ (2.11)

Theorem 4.1 (Unified Lyapunov descent) . Under Assumption 2.1 and the parameter choice ( 4.3 ), Algorithm 1 satisfies $\mathcal{V}_{t}\geq 0$ for every $t$ . Moreover, $\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{t+1}-\mathcal{V}_{t}\leq-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{D}_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1},w_{t})-\frac{\beta}{8L}\|\nabla p(z_{t})\|^{2}.$ (4.7) In particular, $\mathcal{V}_{t+1}-\mathcal{V}_{t}\leq-\frac{\beta}{8L}\|\nabla p(z_{t})\|^{2}.$ (4.8)

Corollary 4.1 . Under the conditions of Theorem 4.1 , the deterministic output satisfies ${\mathcal{R}(x_{\rm out},y_{\rm out})\leq\sqrt{S_{j}}+\tau\|y_{j+1}\|\leq\sqrt{\frac{32L\Delta_{\tau}}{\beta T}}+\tau D_{Y}.}$ (4.12) The random output $z_{\rm out}\in X$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}\|\nabla p(z_{\rm out})\|^{2}\leq\frac{8L\Delta_{\tau}}{\beta T}$ (4.13) and $\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi_{2L}(z_{\rm out})\|^{2}\leq\frac{16L\Delta_{\tau}}{\beta T}+8L\tau D_{Y}^{2}.$ (4.14)

Theorem 4.2 (Nonconvex–strongly concave optimization-stationarity complexity) . Suppose that Assumption 2.1 holds with $\mu>0$ . For $\varepsilon>0$ , let $\tau=0$ , $\mu_{y}=\mu$ , and $\lambda=2L$ , and choose the remaining parameters as in ( 4.3 ). Run Algorithm 1 for $T=\max\left\{1,\left\lceil\frac{128L\Delta_{0}}{\beta\varepsilon^{2}}\right\rceil\right\}$ (4.15) iterations. The random center returned by Algorithm 1 satisfies $\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi_{2L}(z_{\rm out})\|^{2}\leq\varepsilon^{2}.$ (4.16)
Remark 4.1 . For fixed $\Delta_{0}>0$ , as $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ , the first-order oracle complexity of Theorem 4.2 is $O\!\left(\sqrt{\kappa}L\Delta_{0}\varepsilon^{-2}\right).$ (4.17)

Theorem 4.3 (Nonconvex–strongly concave game-stationarity complexity) . Under the assumptions and parameter choices of Theorem 4.2 , run Algorithm 1 for $T$ iterations, with $T$ given by ( 4.15 ). The deterministic game output satisfies $\mathcal{R}(x_{\rm out},y_{\rm out})\leq\varepsilon.$ (4.18)
Remark 4.2 . For fixed $\Delta_{0}>0$ , as $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ , the first-order oracle complexity of Theorem 4.3 is $O\!\left(\sqrt{\kappa}L\Delta_{0}\varepsilon^{-2}\right).$ (4.19)

Theorem 4.4 (Nonconvex–concave optimization-stationarity complexity) . Suppose that Assumption 2.1 holds with $\mu=0$ . For $\varepsilon>0$ , let $\tau=\min\left\{L,\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{16LD_{Y}^{2}}\right\},\qquad\mu_{y}=\tau,$ (4.22) let $\lambda=2L$ , and choose the remaining parameters as in ( 4.3 ). Run Algorithm 1 for $T=\max\left\{1,\left\lceil\frac{128L\Delta_{\tau}}{\beta\varepsilon^{2}}\right\rceil\right\}$ (4.23) iterations. The random output of Algorithm 1 satisfies $\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi_{2L}(z_{\rm out})\|^{2}\leq\varepsilon^{2}.$ (4.24)

Remark 4.3 . By Lemma 4.4 and the choice of $\tau$ , $\Delta_{\tau}\leq\bar{\Delta}_{0}+O(\varepsilon^{2}/L)$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ . For fixed $\bar{\Delta}_{0}>0$ , the first-order oracle complexity of Theorem 4.4 is therefore $O\!\left(L^{2}D_{Y}\bar{\Delta}_{0}\varepsilon^{-3}\right).$ (4.25)

Theorem 4.5 (Nonconvex–concave game-stationarity complexity) . Suppose that Assumption 2.1 holds with $\mu=0$ . For $\varepsilon>0$ , let $\tau=\min\left\{L,\frac{\varepsilon}{2D_{Y}}\right\},\qquad\mu_{y}=\tau,$ (4.26) let $\lambda=2L$ , and choose the remaining parameters as in ( 4.3 ). Run Algorithm 1 for $T$ iterations, with $T$ given by ( 4.23 ) using the present values of $\beta$ and $\Delta_{\tau}$ . The deterministic game output of Algorithm 1 satisfies $\mathcal{R}(x_{\rm out},y_{\rm out})\leq\varepsilon.$ (4.27)

Remark 4.4 . By Lemma 4.4 and the choice of $\tau$ , $\Delta_{\tau}\leq\bar{\Delta}_{0}+O(\varepsilon D_{Y})$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ . For fixed $\bar{\Delta}_{0}>0$ , the first-order oracle complexity of Theorem 4.5 is therefore $O\!\left(L^{3/2}D_{Y}^{1/2}\bar{\Delta}_{0}\varepsilon^{-5/2}\right).$ (4.28)

Corollary 4.2 (Warm-started NC–SC complexity) . Suppose that $\mu>0$ . Set $\tau=0$ , $\eta=\varepsilon^{2}/L$ , and $\kappa=L/\mu$ , and write $\overline{H}_{\mu}:=\overline{H}_{\mu,0}$ . Algorithm 2 returns a random OS center and a deterministic GS pair satisfying $\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi_{2L}(z_{\rm out})\|^{2}\leq\varepsilon^{2},\qquad\mathcal{R}(x_{\rm out},y_{\rm out})\leq\varepsilon.$ (4.39) Its oracle complexity is $N=O\!\left(\sqrt{\kappa}\left[\frac{L\Delta_{\phi}}{\varepsilon^{2}}+1+\log\!\left(1+\frac{L\overline{H}_{\mu}}{\varepsilon^{2}}\right)\right]\right).$ (4.40) For a fixed instance with $\Delta_{\phi}>0$ , the leading term is $O(\sqrt{\kappa}L\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-2})$ .

Corollary 4.3 (Warm-started NC–C optimization stationarity) . Suppose that $\mu=0$ . Choose $\tau$ as in ( 4.22 ) and set $\eta=\tau D_{Y}^{2}$ . Algorithm 2 returns a random center satisfying $\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi_{2L}(z_{\rm out})\|^{2}\leq\varepsilon^{2}.$ (4.41) The full query bound is ( 4.38 ), with $B_{0,\tau,\eta}=\Delta_{\phi}+3\tau D_{Y}^{2}/2$ . For a fixed instance with $\Delta_{\phi}>0$ , its leading order as $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ is $O\!\left(L^{2}D_{Y}\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-3}\right).$ (4.42)

Corollary 4.4 (Warm-started NC–C game stationarity) . Suppose that $\mu=0$ . Choose $\tau$ as in ( 4.26 ) and set $\eta=\tau D_{Y}^{2}$ . Algorithm 2 returns a deterministic pair satisfying $\mathcal{R}(x_{\rm out},y_{\rm out})\leq\varepsilon.$ (4.43) The full query bound is again ( 4.38 ), with $B_{0,\tau,\eta}=\Delta_{\phi}+3\tau D_{Y}^{2}/2$ . For a fixed instance with $\Delta_{\phi}>0$ , its leading order as $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ is $O\!\left(L^{3/2}D_{Y}^{1/2}\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-5/2}\right).$ (4.44)

Remark 4.5 (Tolerance and budget information) . The positive tolerance $\eta$ is distinct from the perturbation parameter $\tau$ . In the NC–C case, $\eta=\tau D_{Y}^{2}$ recovers the original warm-up target; in the NC–SC case, $\tau=0$ and this target must be replaced by a positive tolerance. The choice $\eta=\varepsilon^{2}/L$ is valid even when $\Delta_{\phi}=0$ . If only a known bound $\overline{\Delta}\geq\Delta_{\phi}$ is available, it may replace $\Delta_{\phi}$ in the budget and complexity statements. In particular, for NC–SC and $\overline{\Delta}>0$ , the alternative $\eta=\overline{\Delta}$ and $B=2\overline{\Delta}$ gives $N=O\!\left(\sqrt{\kappa}\left[\frac{L\overline{\Delta}}{\varepsilon^{2}}+1+\log\max\{1,\overline{H}_{\mu}/\overline{\Delta}\}\right]\right),$ (4.45) whose warm-up length is independent of $\varepsilon$ . Neither version evaluates the envelope or its infimum. The additive terms in the full bounds cannot be discarded for a zero gap or unbounded initialization errors.

Definition 5.1 (Projected zero-respecting first-order method) . Let $\mathcal{Z}=\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}\times Y$ and $F(x,y)=(\nabla_{x}f(x,y),-\nabla_{y}f(x,y))$ . A deterministic method starts at $w^{0}=0$ and queries $F$ at feasible points $w^{t}\in\mathcal{Z}$ . It is projected zero-respecting if each subsequent query satisfies $\begin{gathered}w^{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{Z}}(a^{t+1}),\\ \supp(a^{t+1})\subseteq\bigcup_{s=0}^{t}\bigl(\supp(w^{s})\cup\supp(F(w^{s}))\bigr).\end{gathered}$ (5.3) After $T$ queries, at $w^{0},\ldots,w^{T-1}$ , its output must also satisfy $\begin{gathered}w^{\mathrm{out}}=\Pi_{\mathcal{Z}}(a^{\mathrm{out}}),\\ \supp(a^{\mathrm{out}})\subseteq\bigcup_{s=0}^{T-1}\bigl(\supp(w^{s})\cup\supp(F(w^{s}))\bigr).\end{gathered}$ (5.4) A primal-only output is permitted if it is the first block of such a $w^{\mathrm{out}}$ . For $T=0$ , the union is empty and the output is the origin. Complexity counts first-order oracle calls; projections are not charged.

Theorem 5.1 (Optimization-stationarity query lower bound) . Let $L_{0}=128$ , $c_{0}=1/512$ , and define $\varepsilon_{*}:=\min\left\{c_{0}\sqrt{\frac{L\Delta}{40L_{0}}},\frac{c_{0}LD_{Y}}{8L_{0}}\right\},\qquad c_{*}:=\frac{c_{0}^{3}}{320L_{0}^{2}}.$ (5.16) For every $0<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_{*}$ , there is an instance satisfying ( 5.1 ), with initial gap $2\Delta/5\leq\Delta_{\phi}\leq\Delta$ , such that any method in Definition 5.1 whose output satisfies ( 5.2 ) must make at least $T\geq c_{*}\frac{L^{2}\Delta_{\phi}D_{Y}}{\varepsilon^{3}}$ (5.17) first-order oracle calls. More precisely, for the dimensions chosen in the proof, every output after $T<M(n+1)$ queries satisfies $\|\nabla\Phi_{2L}(x^{\mathrm{out}})\|>2\varepsilon$ .

Remark 5.1 (Randomized outputs) . The support induction and Moreau-gradient barrier hold pathwise. For randomized methods satisfying ( 5.3 )–( 5.4 ) almost surely, any fixed query budget $T<M(n+1)$ therefore gives $\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi_{2L}(x^{\mathrm{out}})\|>2\varepsilon,\qquad\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi_{2L}(x^{\mathrm{out}})\|^{2}>4\varepsilon^{2}.$ Thus the lower bound also holds for the expected-norm OS criterion in Definition 2.1 and the expected squared-norm criterion in Theorem 4.4 , at a fixed total query budget.

Remark 5.2 (Matching the upper bound) . The leading OS upper bound ( 4.42 ) for Algorithm 2 matches the lower bound in Theorem 5.1 in its $L^{2}D_{Y}\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-3}$ dependence within the class of projected zero-respecting methods. The additional terms in ( 4.38 ) are lower order for each fixed instance with $\Delta_{\phi}>0$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ . Appendix 11.4 verifies the initialization and oracle-class conditions required for this comparison.

Theorem 9.1 . For each iteration $t$ , the update from $w_{t}$ to $w_{t+1}$ at the fixed center $z_{t}$ satisfies $\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1})-\mathcal{E}_{z_{t}}(w_{t})+\frac{\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{256L^{2}}\bigl(\|v_{t+1}\|^{2}-\|v_{t}\|^{2}\bigr)$ (9.21) $\displaystyle+\frac{h\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{32}\left[\mathcal{E}_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1})+\frac{\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{256L^{2}}\|v_{t+1}\|^{2}\right]\leq-\mathcal{D}_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1},w_{t}).$ Both terms in brackets are nonnegative by Lemma 9.2 .

Remark 10.1 (Budget from an initial-energy upper bound) . The budget does not require computing $\Delta_{0}$ exactly. Given any known $\overline{\Delta}_{0}\geq\Delta_{0}$ , choose instead $T=\max\left\{1,\left\lceil\frac{128L\overline{\Delta}_{0}}{\beta\varepsilon^{2}}\right\rceil\right\}.$ (10.15) The conclusions of Theorems 4.2 and 4.3 then hold, and for fixed $\overline{\Delta}_{0}>0$ the complexity as $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ is $O\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{L}{\mu}}\,\frac{L\overline{\Delta}_{0}}{\varepsilon^{2}}\right)$ (10.16) first-order oracle calls. This follows from the same proof by using $\Delta_{0}\leq\overline{\Delta}_{0}$ in the two summation estimates. Thus an available upper bound suffices to prescribe the run length, without evaluating the envelope or its infimum.

Remark 10.2 (Optimal accuracy dependence under strong concavity) . The $\varepsilon^{-2}$ accuracy dependence is optimal with the regularity and initialization bounds fixed. To see this, embed a smooth nonconvex minimization instance $g$ into $f(x,y)=g(x)-\mu\|y\|^{2}/2$ , with $X=\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and a fixed compact convex $Y$ containing $0$ . Then $\phi=g$ , and the game residual controls $\|
abla g(x)\|$ . For OS, let $u=\operatorname{prox}_{g/(2L)}(z)$ . Proximal optimality and smoothness give $
abla\Phi_{2L}(z)=
abla g(u)=2L(z-u),\qquad\|
abla g(z)\|\leq	frac{3}{2}\|
abla\Phi_{2L}(z)\|.$ This pointwise inequality also transfers an expected squared-norm guarantee. Initialize $z_{0}=x_{0}$ , $y_{0}=0$ , and the normal and momentum variables at zero. The definition of $\Delta_{0}$ and the gradient-gap inequality imply $\Delta_{0}\leq g(x_{0})-\inf g+ rac{\|
abla g(x_{0})\|^{2}}{L}\leq 3 igl(g(x_{0})-\inf g igr).$ The smooth-minimization lower bound of Carmon et al. (2020) therefore applies under a common bounded initialization budget. This establishes optimality of the accuracy exponent, without asserting optimality of the condition-number dependence.

Remark 10.3 (Dependence on the condition number) . Writing $\kappa=L/\mu$ , Theorems 4.2 and 4.3 give a baseline gradient complexity upper bound of order $1+\sqrt{\kappa}L\Delta_{0}\varepsilon^{-2}$ for each stated output criterion. Corollary 4.2 replaces $\Delta_{0}$ in the leading term by $\Delta_{\phi}$ , with an additive initialization cost. An optimality comparison must retain both the stationarity criterion and the initialization quantity: lower bounds expressed through the gradient of the value function do not, by themselves, establish a matching lower bound for either guarantee stated here.
